about: Caveats: what a kind of record does not prove, one text per artifact or event type, each with its sources. A record matches the first row whose match fits it: its artifact, and where given its event code, its channel, its time's meaning (ts_desc, for a registry entry's own times), or a word in its registry path. The same record always shows the same text, and the app writes none of it. A source has a title and either a url, for a public page, or a path, which names a file of this app.

caveats.name: Prefetch
caveats.text: A Prefetch file shows the program ran, with up to its last eight run times (Windows 8 and later). It does not show who ran it, or that the run succeeded. A missing .pf file does not mean the program never ran: Prefetch is off by default on Windows Server and may be off on SSDs.

caveats.name: Amcache file entry
caveats.text: An Amcache file entry shows the file was present and inventoried, with its SHA-1. On Windows 10 and later it does not by itself show that the program ran, or who ran it. The time is when Windows' inventory task wrote the entry, not when the file first appeared or ran. The SHA-1 covers only the first 30 MB of the file. Look for Prefetch, a process creation event, or SRUM to show execution.

sources.title: SANS FOR508 syllabus (public page), the disagreement

caveats.name: AppCompatCache entry's file modified time
caveats.text: This time is the file's last modified time as the AppCompatCache entry recorded it, not when Windows saw the file or when the program ran. Compare it with the file's own modified time: if they differ, the file at that path, or its time, changed after the entry was written. On Vista and later the entry does not by itself show that the program ran.

caveats.name: AppCompatCache (Shimcache)
caveats.text: An AppCompatCache entry shows Windows saw the file. On Vista and later it does not by itself show that the program ran. The row's time is the cache key's last write, shared by every entry on the host, so it is not when this file was seen or run. The file's modified time is in the entry's data. Windows writes the cache to the registry only at a clean shutdown.

sources.title: The Stolen Szechuan Sauce case (DFIR Madness): in a Glessner case built from DC01 and DESKTOP, each host's AppCompatCache rows share one time

caveats.name: UserAssist and BAM last run time
caveats.text: This is the last run time the entry records for the program, under the account its key belongs to. Earlier runs leave no time here. On Windows 10 and later, UserAssist can set its last run time when the program did not run. UserAssist records programs started from the Windows GUI. BAM may not record every program that ran. This time does not show that a run succeeded or what the program did.

caveats.name: SAM account times

ts_desc: SAM account name key last write

caveats.text: These times come from this host's SAM hive, which holds the host's local accounts only, not domain accounts. The name key last write is when the account's key under SAM\Domains\Account\Users\Names last changed. A later write moves it, so it can come after the account was made. A last logon time is the latest logon the record holds. These times do not show who used the account, or from where. Look for a logon event to show where a logon came from.

sources.title: Microsoft, Credentials processes in Windows authentication: Security Accounts Manager database
Windows Incident Response, User Account Analysis (Carvey, 2009)
Windows Registry knowledge base, SAM Domains key: Users RID sub key F value
The Data Leakage Case (NIST CFReDS): in a Glessner case built from it, the Administrator account's name key last write is 2015-03-25, after its last logon in 2010

caveats.name: USB and SCSI device times
caveats.text: These times come from the device's entry in the SYSTEM hive. The first installed time is when Windows first installed the device. The installed time is when Windows last installed the device's driver, so a driver update moves it. The last connected and last removed times are the latest connection and removal the entry holds. These times do not show what was copied to or from the device, who connected it, or its connections between the first install and the last connection. Windows 7 records no last connection or removal time. A major Windows update can remove a USB device's entry and its times.

sources.title: Yogesh Khatri's forensic blog, Windows 8 device timestamps (Khatri, 2013)
0x55aa, Windows feature updates and USB devices (Kobzar, 2021)
13Cubed, Windows Registry Cheat Sheet (version 2.0): USBSTOR's Properties times

caveats.name: Entry key last write

ts_desc: Volume info cache key last write

caveats.text: This time is when the entry's own registry key last changed. It does not show what changed, or when the entry was first made: a later update, or a setting written again, moves it.

sources.title: The Data Leakage Case (NIST CFReDS): in a Glessner case built from it, a USB drive's Device Classes keys were last written when it was connected again on 2015-03-24, not at its first connection the day before

caveats.name: ProfileList logon and logoff times
caveats.text: These times come from the account's key under ProfileList in the SOFTWARE hive. The last logon time is when the profile service last loaded the account's profile. The last logoff time is when it last unloaded the profile. Windows 10 version 1809, Windows Server 2019, and later versions record them. Earlier loads and unloads leave no time here. These times do not show where a logon came from. Look for a logon event to show that. RECmd writes about 1 in 16 of these times with a year before 1829, since it drops the leading zeros of the time's low half. The app rebuilds those times, so the event's time can differ from the LastLogonTime or LastLogoffTime in its details.

sources.title: Microsoft, Scripts to retrieve profile age: LocalProfileLoadTime and LocalProfileUnloadTime

caveats.name: Office file opened and closed times
caveats.text: The last opened time comes from the file's entry in the Office program's MRU list, in the account's NTUSER hive. Office updates that time each time the file is opened. Earlier opens leave no time here. The last closed time is the last write of the file's entry under the program's Reading Locations key. Word writes that entry when a document is closed. An MRU entry stays after its file is deleted, so it does not show that the file still exists.

sources.title: Cyber Triage, What is a Most Recently Used artifact (video)
ThinkDFIR, Microsoft Office Reading Locations, part 1 (Moore, 2019)

caveats.name: Typed URL time
caveats.text: This time comes from the URL's value in the TypedURLsTime key, beside TypedURLs in the account's NTUSER hive. It is when the URL was entered in Internet Explorer's address bar. In tests of Internet Explorer 6 and 8, a URL typed in full, completed by AutoComplete, or picked from the address bar's list got an entry. A pasted URL got one once Enter was pressed. So the time does not show that the user typed the whole URL. A link followed from a page added no entry. The list kept 25 URLs and dropped older ones. Clearing the browsing history cleared it.

sources.title: Champlain College Leahy Center, Windows 8 Forensics Part 2 (Fleisher, 2012)
Crucial Security Forensics Blog, TypedURLs part 1 (Nichols, 2011)

caveats.name: MRU list times
caveats.text: This time is the last write of the MRU list's registry key. RECmd gives it to the list's newest entry, the first in the list's order. The list's other entries get no time. A key's last write is the last time the key or any of its values changed. Deleting another entry also moves it, so the time may not be when this entry was used. The RecentDocs extension time is the last write of the extension's own key, given to that extension's newest entry. Creating a file adds a RecentDocs entry even if the file is never opened.

sources.title: Magnet Forensics, What is MRU (Most Recently Used)? (2022)
Forensic 4:cast, Updates to the RecentDocs key in Windows 10 (Whitfield, 2019)

caveats.name: Scheduled task times
caveats.text: These times come from the DynamicInfo value of the task's key under TaskCache\Tasks in the SOFTWARE hive. The created time is when the task was created. One format reference marks it as possibly the last registration or update, so it may come after the task was first made. The last started time is the task's last run. Earlier runs leave no time here. The last stopped time is when a run last finished. It does not show that the run succeeded. In a published test, a run of a task whose program did not exist still set it. The last run's result code is in the details as LastActionResult. Windows 7 records no last stopped time.

sources.title: Windows Registry knowledge base, Task scheduler keys: DynamicInfo

caveats.name: JumplistData time
caveats.text: This time is the data of the program's value under Search\JumplistData in the account's NTUSER hive. RECmd's plugin and batch file describe it as the program's last execution time. No other public page found explains what writes it. The key keeps one time per program.

caveats.name: Remote Desktop server key last write

ts_desc: Remote Desktop server entry last modified

caveats.text: This time is the last write of the server's key under Terminal Server Client\Servers in the account's NTUSER hive. Connecting to the server with the Remote Desktop Connection client (mstsc) creates the key and sets its UsernameHint value. A key's last write is the last time the key or any of its values changed. The key keeps no time for each connection, so this time does not show the first connection or how many there were.

sources.title: JPCERT/CC, Tool Analysis Result Sheet: mstsc (RDP)

caveats.name: RADAR last detection time
caveats.text: This time is the LastDetectionTime value of the program's key under RADAR\HeapLeakDetection\DiagnosedApplications in the SOFTWARE hive. Windows' memory leak diagnoser sets it when it picks a running process that has committed at least a set share of the host's physical memory. So the program was running at this time, but the time is not when it started. Only programs that commit that much memory get an entry. So a missing entry does not show that a program never ran.

sources.title: Harel Segev, The mystery of the HeapLeakDetection registry key (2022)

caveats.name: Shortcut (LNK) and jump list
caveats.text: A shortcut or jump list entry shows the shell recorded a reference to the file under that profile. Applications, File and Open dialogs, drag and drop, and programs also create entries, so it does not prove the user opened the file on purpose, or that the program ran. It does not show that the file still exists, or what it contained.

caveats.name: Logon events 4624 and 4625
caveats.text: A logon event shows an account authenticated, or failed to, from a source. It does not show who used the account. On an NTLM logon, the workstation name is the one the client sent. The address and workstation fields depend on the authentication protocol.

caveats.name: Autoruns entry
caveats.text: An Autoruns entry shows a persistence location and its target. It does not show when the entry was set. For a program file the time is when the linker built the image, for a script it is the file's last write, and for a location row it is the key's or folder's last change.

sources.title: parsers/autoruns.py, header comment on the Time column

caveats.name: Suricata alert
caveats.text: An alert shows that traffic matched a signature. It does not show that the attack succeeded. The alert's source address is not necessarily the attacker.

sources.title: UCSB, Using Alert Verification to Identify Successful Intrusion Attempts (Kruegel, Robertson, and Vigna, 2004)

caveats.name: Service installed (7045)
caveats.text: A 7045 shows a service was registered with its image path. It does not show the binary ran. The account shown is the one the event's System element names. In the EVTX-ATTACK-SAMPLES events checked, that was the account that installed the service. This is inference beyond those samples. It is not the account the service runs as. Look for the file's creation, a Prefetch or process creation for the path, and the logon before it.

sources.title: EVTX-ATTACK-SAMPLES, Lateral Movement folder, LM_Remote_Service02_7045.evtx: the account in the System element of its 7045 events
